Our proposal results in a sophisticated framework that resolves classic paradoxes like Russell's paradox by enabling partial truths within sets. This new theory has intriguing implications for the distribution of sets over natural numbers, enabling a solution to the continuum hypothesis.

Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces and signal processing technology enable the continuous analysis of brain signals to estimate key parameters of a person's movement, including walking speed and stride length. Our research builds upon this by introducing a novel method to forecast ambulatory states and stride frequency from local electrical brain activity measured via an electrocorticogram, a direct reading of brain electrical activity. Our approach combines artificial neural networks with spectral features from continuous, 64-channel ECoG signals, successfully predicting ambulatory states and stride frequency in both healthy individuals and stroke patients who have undergone surgical brain implantation. The results demonstrate accurate predictions when using real-time data, indicating potential for the development of a brain-based system to monitor patients' rehabilitation progress during ambulatory activities outside of a controlled laboratory setting.

This paper introduces a new computational approach to estimating the entropy of diverse probability distributions by leveraging the Nested Sampling method. Initially developed for evaluating expectations in complex scenarios, our proposed algorithm builds upon this framework to calculate integrals related to entropy formulas, ultimately yielding an efficient entropy estimation technique. By harnessing the power of Nested Sampling, our approach enables us to efficiently evaluate entropy quantities even when dealing with highly intricate probability distributions that cannot be easily managed through conventional analytical methods. To illustrate the benefits of this approach, we demonstrate its application by estimating entropy measures for both simple and complex examples, including distributions of random matrices, and intriguing scenarios of random fractals, showcasing notable time complexity improvements over traditional methods.

Minimally generated finite groups that contain no copies of A times the cyclic group Z have no nontrivial subgroups containing elements of infinite order. We employ this property to create a new class of groups that cannot contain nontrivial finite subgroups. By combining it with the property of being minimally generated, we obtain a new class of groups that cannot contain nontrivial finite subgroups and cannot contain elements of infinite order within any of their proper subgroups. We establish that right-angled Artin groups containing a connected graph with more than one component satisfy this condition. We use this result to develop a novel method for creating subgroup systems and diverse intertribe distances in right-angled Artin groups. Specifically, for any positive integer k, we construct a collection of k pairwise independent subgroups within the right-angled Artin group associated with a fully transitive graph on 11 vertices. Our construction surpasses prior work on this subject.

In our proposed approach, we develop a novel non-parametric method using pairwise and long-range comparisons to effectively identify dynamic functional connections between time-series variables. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated across different data sets and under varying conditions, outperforming traditional state-based and comparison-based methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Our research findings are further supported by theoretical complexity analyses, indicating our method's optimal connection discovery performance and low computational cost. Implementations of our approach are made available for public use.

Phylogenetic networks serve as a detailed representation of the evolutionary histories of various species, enabling them to incorporate reticulate evolutionary mechanisms such as lateral gene transfer and gene recombination. In contrast to phylogenetic trees, these networks provide a more comprehensive view of the evolutionary process. Creating software tools that accurately reconstruct these networks of evolution is a pressing need, as the species that benefit from them are increasingly diverse, including plants, animals, and microorganisms. Notably, next-generation sequencing technologies produce vast amounts of data that can construct networks with a level of resolution previously unattainable, with each taxon now being represented by thousands of gene sequences rather than single characters. Given this context, it is surprising that there has been little comparison made so far between the topological characteristics of sets of phylogenetic trees that are generated using different methods, particularly network construction algorithms, despite such comparisons being necessary to validate the efficacy of these methods in producing accurate results. This study seeks to address this shortfall by comparing the topological features of the phylogenetic trees that are generated using different network construction algorithms, with a focus on DGE Network, TESS, and SplitTree. To accomplish this, we utilized a comprehensive dataset consisting of 104 organisms from 19 distinct taxonomic groups, examining 10 different topological characteristics in detail. Our results reveal that the phylogenetic trees produced by DGE Network exhibit the shortest heights, as well as the fewest internal nodes and the longest external branches

In observing insect behavior, a common technique used is the flash photo method. A computational approach developed in this study transforms video footage from this method into a usable format for analyzing movement of live subjects. A novel detection algorithm created for this purpose automatically identifies and tracks the movement of live organisms across video clips. The algorithm's performance was tested with data sets from four different species of crickets, with the results showing a high level of accuracy in measuring movement when compared to traditional methods used in biological research.

Neural network training often employs matrix inversion methods, like conjugate gradient and banded techniques. However, these methods typically have a limited number of iterations due to their high computational cost, leading us to investigate faster iterative alternatives. Building on Krylov-based methods and leveraging matrix-vector operations optimized for GPU architecture, we propose a new framework for matrix inversion. Specifically, we explore the use of neural network layer functions as surrogates for matrix-vector products and demonstrate that exact inversion is possible by stacking these maps. Our approach facilitates efficient matrix inversion for large sparse matrices, even those with non-zero diagonal elements, by drawing from the Neumann series. We apply this framework to neural network training, leveraging GPU-optimized matrix-vector operations through the NNVM tensor computation framework. Our results show that it supports ResNet-110 for 6000 CIFAR-10 images and has similar classification accuracy to TensorFlow.

For systems that scatter waves, additional properties can be defined to further analyze energy distribution patterns. These properties, referred to as eigenchannels, detail how energy is dispersed in scattered waves. Specifically, a novel framework identifies energy patterns based on relative strengths of wave scattering at different locations. The framework's utility is demonstrated through a practical application involving sound wave scattering in a complex fluid dynamics scenario. Calculations using the proposed method accurately predict energy absorption rates in turbulent turbulent mixing layers behind vortex pairs that interact mechanically. The method effectively accounts for the systems' complexity, capturing the transition from strong to weak coupling between vortex pairs. The results show that reducing coupling between the vortex pairs increases energy absorption in the outer channel, while also leading to heightened energy transfer from the inner channel. The method is also compared to a simpler approach, revealing that the new framework provides a more detailed understanding of energy transfer and absorption. The results are validated through experimental measurements and direct simulations. The method is highly versatile and can be applied to a wide range of systems involving the scattering of wave fields.

We examine topological Anderson insulators in one-dimensional piecewise
linear conductors with binary disorders and investigate how the random
inclusions affect their topological properties. Our study demonstrates that
critical points, where a topological phase transition occurs, can be
located through the disorder-averaged carrier localization lengths in an
quasi-periodic potential. Furthermore, we analyze how different disorder
symmetries influence the topological Anderson phases, revealing that the
phases can be isolated and distinguished by the average localization
lengths in both uniform and quasi-periodic potentials. Our research shows
that time-reversal symmetry is sufficient but not necessary for the
topological Anderson phases to emerge. Additionally, we find that the
phases can be stabilized in isolated clusters by adjusting the disorder
strength.

Trim sequences form a distinguished class within the broader category of unicellular structures, characterized by exclusive use of the left fork operation in combinatorial structures such as binary trees and planar pointed trees. The term "trim" was first introduced by Mierkats in 2019 in the context of combinatorics. This paper introduces the concept of a trim structure in graph theory and explores connections to the combinatorial version. Specifically, it establishes a bijection between the set of planar pointed trees and the set of combinatorial trim sequences. This bijection employs the EGP involution to derive a Gallois link between the automorphism groups of these structures. Additionally, this paper explores implications for structures like binary trees and provides a formula for counting the number of combinatorial trim sequences.

Within the Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model, the on-shell effective Lagrangian approach simplifies the complex renormalizable theory to a more manageable, two-loop Lagrangian involving the Higgs sector and its interactions with other fields. A key characteristic of this approach is the appearance of unwanted, quadratic divergences related to the Higgs naturalization process. In the present study, we tackle the challenge of systematically removing these unwanted divergences to ensure the Higgs parameters remain finite and physically meaningful. Our findings also reveal intriguing patterns of cancellation of the quadratic divergences, which stem from the intricate nature of the renormalizable theory. Ultimately, our research provides a clear framework for extracting the finite, physically relevant parameters of the on-shell effective Lagrangian directly from the infinite set of Lagrangian parameters, encompassing both the Higgs sector and the rest of the theory.

Conditional independence between features and historical values of a time series, given past innovations, is a fundamental assumption in linearity tests for time series models. Although this condition may not always hold true, researchers have developed innovative approaches to circumvent it. Leveraging simulations and real-world data, our paper examines the performance of four advanced linearity tests for network autoregressive models, including the test proposed by Arai and Kanamori, as well as their extensions. Our findings highlight significant improvements in test statistics and asymptotic standardisation when employing the scores approach. We also delve into the benefits of using the minimum eigenvalue estimator and demonstrate its robustness through sensitivity analysis. Furthermore, our results indicate mixed outcomes for the other linearity tests. Additionally, we investigate the ease of implementation, computational speed, and interpretability of the test statistics and asymptotic standardisation. Overall, our research suggests that linearity be assessed through a combination of various approaches given the limitations of the tests examined here.

In this study, we introduce a novel methodology using Issue-Frameworks for Factual Validation (If4FV) to assess the factual accuracy of neural network-generated text. We employ If4FV to investigate two areas of research: knowledge-based neural networks with focused question-answering tasks and realistic neural network-generated text. If4FV's effectiveness is demonstrated through two exploratory studies, and our approach is made available open-source for future research to build upon our findings.

A versatile framework is introduced that effectively models the movement of cells and the redistribution of proteins on membranes moving due to external forces. This framework's versatility stems from its ability to handle various cell and protein movement patterns, including directed motion, diffusion and advection. By combining reaction-diffusion equations that account for cell and protein movement, this framework's usefulness can be further expanded through the application of suitable simplifications and approximations. As a result, a novel approach is provided for tackling problems involving the interaction of cells with external fluid flows. Key challenges arise when attempting to interpret data from experiments that observe cells' behavior under flow conditions, and our model offers a valuable tool for achieving this goal.

This study focuses on uncovering the underlying causes of malicious activities within cryptocurrency systems. Our analysis reveals that malicious transactions are frequently linked to specific 'financial roadmaps', with certain patterns emerging across various types of attacks. Our system, designed to detect and interpret these patterns within a cryptocurrency network, utilizes machine learning to classify transactions as part of a known attack pattern or a new unidentified roadmap. Our implementation, comprising a machine learning-based classifier and a graph-based analysis tool, successfully identified 14 distinct attack patterns and demonstrated the ability to detect a previously unknown roadmap associated with the Ryuk ransomware attack. By detecting financial roadmaps, our system can provide valuable insights for security researchers, helping them to better comprehend the evolutionary patterns of attacks and ultimately contributing to a more secure cryptocurrency ecosystem.

Large-scale quantum computing requires encoded qubits to withstand errors from the interaction between qubits and a noisy environment. In this context, we develop a coding framework based on reinforcement learning for fault-tolerant quantum computing. By viewing the encoding process as a series of single-qubit operations and quantum gate applications, we define a coding protocol that protects qubits from error caused by single-qubit rotations. Formulating the decoding process as a reward-based learning problem, we use reinforcement learning to develop codes that effectively minimize the error in the decoded qubit state. Building upon this foundation, we explore extensions to more complex quantum circuits, considering bounds on the number of stable qubits and encoding/decoding operations, and assess code performance with respect to error types and quantum circuit complexity. Our coding protocols, precluding the utilization of error correction codes like the surface code, offer promising code examples suitable for execution on devices like the superconducting quantum processor, enabling nearly error-free execution of critical quantum functions for cryptography.

Quantum metrology enhances measurement precision by leveraging the interplay of quantum phenomena. We investigate an unusual scenario where two interconnected cavities contain highly entangled states. Our focus is on how this quantum state of entanglement affects the estimation of a single unknown variable. Initial research analyzed this problem for independent cavities; however, we explore its implications in an interconnected scenario, identifying specific conditions under quantum leap metrology. Furthermore, we demonstrate that interconnection can both hinder and facilitate metrological advancements, depending on various factors.

Researchers calculated direct photon-hadron correlations in Au+Au and d+Au collisions at 200 GeV to study jet interactions with the medium. Comparing results to p+p collisions allowed for an adjustment of systematic biases. After accounting for bias and flow-related effects, the analysis revealed a notable difference between Au+Au and p+p collisions. Specifically, the influence of flow on the distribution of hadrons relative to direct photons was more pronounced in Au+Au collisions. Furthermore, the presence of a medium-induced shift in the distribution of hadrons relative to direct photons was observed in Au+Au collisions but not in d+Au collisions, providing insight into jet-medium interactions in nuclear collisions.

This paper proposes a novel mathematical concept, the universal Smarandache sigma product of figures, and derives a fundamental formula for computing its value. Additionally, we prove a theorem demonstrating the intimacy between the universal Smarandache sigma product of figures and the conventional concept of integer factorization.

Illuminating the unknowns of cloud network system soundness, our research uncovers the unexplored relationship between network performance variability and the scalability of distributed applications. Through analysis and proof of concept in both theoretical and practical settings, our findings highlight the inadequacy of current measurement techniques in capturing essential variables and propose an empirical framework for evaluating soundness in cloud environments. Additionally, we introduce novel metrics and methods for assessing the impact of variable network performance on application scalability and provide a prototype system for conducting such evaluations. By addressing the challenges posed by variable network performance, our research offers actionable recommendations for achieving better soundness in cloud deployments.

Agents making decisions in a series of independent rounds can benefit from a framework called distributed contextual linear gambits. The agent, also known as the learner, observes features and makes decisions based on an unknown context, while other agents, called experts, provide recommendations based on the features alone. The experts do not need to share the context with the learner. A recent breakthrough established a minimal information transfer mechanism by providing the experts' average recommendations to the learner. However, this breakthrough required the context to be known to the learner. Our research focuses on addressing the original unbounded contextual case. We establish multiple main results including: firstly, achieving a minimal information transfer by providing specific average recommendations from individual experts to the learner; secondly, developing an approximately optimal policy when the context is known to the learner; and lastly, developing an approximately optimal policy when the context is not known to the learner by leveraging results from the first case. Our research provides the first solutions to the original unbounded contextual case.

Our research investigates how telecommuting influences Scrum project success, a topic widely discussed in the IT industry but not thoroughly studied in the Scrum framework context. We employed both a systematic review and a case study to achieve a deeper understanding of this topic. The review of 42 international journals revealed that telecommuting's effectiveness in Scrum project success depends on factors such as team dynamics, communication, and conflict management. Additionally, our case study of two software development teams allowed us to explore additional aspects, including trust, trustworthiness, and spatial work environment factors. Our findings provide a theoretical framework that can be useful for software development project managers navigating the shift to remote work and working from home.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy evaluation efficiency in complex settings. Building upon the work of Kallus (2020), we develop efficient algorithms for identifying individualized treatment rules in distributionally robust settings, specifically addressing categorical observations and future observations. Our results are distinctive in addressing observed categorical data, a widely occurring phenomenon in practice. For future observations, our results complement and build upon the findings of Kallus (2020). Both new results are accompanied by numerical experiments highlighting the effectiveness of proposed methods.

This paper presents AMPT model simulations of full Pb-Pb collisions at a 2.76 TeV energy level, with an emphasis on 2.4 to 4.5 GeV p~$y$~scale and elliptic movement effects in final particle distributions. Elliptic movement is shown to significantly impact particle spectra, often masking AMPT's natural trends. By accounting for initial state anisotropies, a better understanding of medium properties is gained. Certain particle species exhibit increased sensitivity to elliptic movement due to initial state anisotropies. Unique features of elliptic movement are best accessed through two-particle correlation functions. The influence of elliptic movement and p~$y$~scales is compared for both AMPT and PHENIX experimental data. Finally, p~$y$~scales of 2.38 and 1.93 are found to distinguish between an anisotropy influenced spectrum and a single freeze-out scenario.

This research develops the quaternionic linear canonical transform (QLCT) on signals and images by extending the conventional LCT. Building upon previous work, we derive key properties and characteristics for the QLCT, including its inverse and a specific indeterminacy principle. Key theorems and lemmas are based on the conventional LCT, yielding results such as linearity, a derived expression for the QLCT, and stability properties. Notably, we introduce a discrete version of the QLCT and demonstrate its efficacy through numerical experiments, showcasing its applicability in signal and image processing.

This work extends our previous finding from a binary power binary interference network that the extremal sum generalization degree of freedom for K user networks can be $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$.  We enhance our previous result by demonstrating that the same $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ extremal sum generalization degree of freedom enhancement is achievable when power regulation is optimal.  We derive a lower bound for the K user case, and develop an upper bound with an extremely large, yet finite, number of users in the scope of a generalized version of a previously constructed code.  Our analysis yields the exact generalization degree of freedom for a duple interference network.  The answer to whether optimal power can be substituted with binary power in a triple interference network remains unanswered.

The growing interest in simulating and modeling complex fluid-particle systems necessitates a new integration method that allows for larger time steps in particle interactions. By redefining the collision duration in relation to the time step used in simulations, a new approach has been developed to create more realistic particle interactions. The proposed method maintains accuracy in simulations by ensuring that particles do not skip over actual collisions, thus preventing errors in predictions of particle behavior, including particle sticking, breaking, and ejection events. Building on previous work, this method has been tested in various scenarios, including demonstrations of particle slipping, particle collisions leading to particle ejection, and simulations of particle flows over longer periods. Results show that this method has a significant impact on predictions of particle behavior, particularly when time steps used in simulations are larger than traditional values required for stable convergence. The development of this method has potential applications in improving predictions of particle behavior in various engineering processes and natural phenomena.
This article presents $3$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the fact that the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ has exactly whole number solutions for $a, b, n$ where $n$ is greater than $1$.

A key challenge in robotics research is for robots to navigate varied terrain efficiently, and to achieve this, it's essential for their motion to be well-understood on different surfaces. This study focuses on a monopod robot that uses a long, thin leg to move by hopping. The surface it operates on is modeled after a type of material that changes shape in response to force and slowness of deformation, and this interaction causes the monopod's footprints to affect its subsequent hopping pattern. Next, the project simulates how the monopod's movement and the surface interact with each other. Interestingly, the model shows that even small changes in the footprints can significantly impact the monopod's hopping pattern. To improve stability, the optimal placement of the monopod's foot is identified through further analysis of the model's dynamics. Finally, the model's ability to model different surface conditions is demonstrated by experimenting with various types of yielding terrain.

In this paper, we use a contact interaction to explain the elastic shape factors of mesons within the context of a unified approach. Initially, we derive formulae for the AdS$_5$ Schr\"{o}dinger mode function and its corresponding WKB approximation. Subsequently, we compare our results to previous works by Giannakis and Semay, obtaining a new, simplified expression for the elastic boomerang factor. Furthermore, our model predicts a relationship between the boomerang and vortex factors in the WKB limit.

A droplet in the presence of a surrounding gas, where there are varying electric field strengths, exhibits a complex behavior of oscillation that is captured by an analytical resonance phenomenon. This resonance occurs when the droplet's natural frequency aligns with the electric field's frequency, causing a pattern of oscillation called a "hydraulic fan". This study aims to provide an initial framework for understanding how droplet movements are affected by an external electric field, a phenomenon observed in spray aerosols.

Effective communication through language cannot be fully achieved without considering negation, a fundamental aspect of all human languages. Despite being present in every language, negation poses significant challenges to current natural language processing systems. To accelerate the advancement of models capable of accurately processing negation, we introduce CONDAQA, a pioneering set of question-answering tasks designed to assess the ability of AI models to grasp the implications of negation in written text. The CONDAQA dataset comprises 12,000 challenging question-answer pairs, carefully crafted to ensure that the correct answer cannot be deduced without fully understanding the negation present in the text. We also outline an initial exploration of models' performance on this dataset, highlighting the limitations of current state-of-the-art models in effectively dealing with negation. Furthermore, we present a novel evaluation metric called Negation-aware Reasoning Score (NRS), tailored to evaluate models' capacity for sound reasoning in the presence of negation.

Computing network structures like cores, quasicores, and condensates has significant implications in various fields due to their relevance in identifying targeted nodes and understanding the underlying geometry of networks. However, current methods often struggle to handle large networks within realistic timeframes. To address this challenge, we introduce an innovative approach based on graph partitioning, which significantly improves performance while retaining accuracy. Our model exhibits superior scalability, with notable applications including the efficient identification of cores in massive networks and the creation of reduced condensates for statistical analysis. By leveraging C++ and Python tools, our approach provides a flexible solution that networks analysts can easily employ.

Quantum annealing shows promise in addressing complex, intractable problems when applying conventional methods. However, the transition to the ground state, necessary for finding equilibrium properties in the quantum system, poses a significant obstacle. This challenge can be circumvented by relying on quench dynamics, which generates the quantum propagator almost instantly. The critical parameter regulating this method is the quantum annealing interval, a feature of our quantum processor, influencing success rates in solving optimization problems through quench dynamics. In this work, we investigate the annealing interval in the context of the exact cover problem, considering which factors affect it and identifying relevant nonequilibrium dynamics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the annealing interval can be optimized to achieve superior outcomes with reduced computational resources, achieving a $O(n^2)$ reduction in variance for large $n$. The developed theoretical framework may be applied to other dichotomous interactions.

This research introduces novel techniques for verifying compliance with patterns in text sequences, specifically focusing on parts of sequences rather than entire sequences. Our approach uses methods from string alignment, particularly infix and postfix alignments, to detect instances of pattern occurrences within any part of the text. We leverage this method to develop tests for checking if a string occurrence fits a pattern by comparing it to a standard reference, and we also explore ways to adapt our approach to accommodate variations in spelling, like those using the Levenshtein distance. We demonstrate the efficiency of our compliance verification method, showing it can handle large text datasets and complex patterns, and even supporting queries using regular expressions. Additionally, we provide examples of applying our technique to instances of pattern matching found in technical documentation, software code, and literary texts.

The capability to control competition between orbital-driven superconductivity and other phenomena, such as charge density waves or magnetism, makes nickelate compounds promising for material science research. By exploring an infinite-layer nickelate with doped holes, we develop a theoretical framework that accounts for both Kondo-lattice and Mott-Hubbard interactions. Our dual-band model is then simplified into a single-band model that captures the essential competition between superconductivity and other phenomena, based on the proximity of the Mott-hubbard peak to the superconducting dome in the phase diagram. Additionally, we demonstrate that this simplification retains the screening of the local moments, which is a critical aspect. The simplified model facilitates numerical analysis of the nickelate's physics within the proximate Mott-hubbard regime.

This research investigates the long-term behavior of initial data with low magnitude in the one-dimensional Boltzmann equation on the whole real line, specifically focusing on the collisionless model. Our findings show that particles spread at a rate governed by $t^2$, with some restrictions, and that certain wave patterns emerge under these conditions. Furthermore, our work establishes that collisions can lead to the emergence of sharp phase differences within the particle distribution.

We use radiance data from space to study the relationship between wind direction and the tilt of ocean waves. By linking the angle of incidence and wind direction, we identify how wind speed influences wave tilt statistics. Our analysis reveals how wave tilt distributions shift in response to increasing wind speed, with a notable change from a bimodal to a unimodal distribution. Our findings challenge existing models of wave tilt statistics.

The growth of diverse software systems necessitates flexible and adaptable testing strategies. One promising approach is the use of uncertainty modeling through fuzzy set theory. Combining fuzzy logic with the Unique Value Decomposition strategy enhances decision-making efficiency. However, applying this method across multiple dimensions in testing scenarios can be computationally intensive. To address this challenge, a parallelized algorithm has been developed to tackle this issue by distributing calculations across multiple processors, significantly reducing processing time. The proposed approach was implemented in a test case selection module for the SOFA software framework, demonstrating a notable increase in processing speed.

The COVID-19 pandemic led to widespread fear and anxiety worldwide, leading to reduced social interactions and a shift to online communication channels. Twitter became a key platform for sharing emotions related to the coronavirus outbreak and measures taken to contain its spread. This study examines sentiment patterns surrounding COVID-19, using a dataset of 300,000 tweets spanning from February to March 2020. A sentiment classification model was trained to classify tweets as positive, negative, or neutral, revealing distinct sentiment patterns tied to specific dates and categories. Findings indicate that emotions expressed during the pandemic lasted for approximately six weeks, peaking in late February and early March 2020. Furthermore, analysis by topic or category showed varying sentiment patterns, with some exhibiting prolonged emotional responses, while others displayed temporary increases in negative feelings.

In cuprate superconductors with an excess of electrons, there's a theoretical gap that could be bridged if certain interlayer conduction models are applicable. Largely based on data from "tunneling" experiments, these models suggest that an unusually large electrical current can flow between copper layers through a specific resonance caused by an unusual electronic state. However, these models have limitations as they don't account for other key experiments and don't provide a clear explanation of how this resonance is triggered. Our research aims to overcome these limitations by integrating elements from both the cuprate and strontium-calcium-copper oxide material groups. By doing so, we've developed a comprehensive theoretical framework that explains how interlayer conduction can occur through a non-resonant mechanism, leveraging a concept called electron-hole pairs that forms an oscillating charge density between copper layers. This new approach is supported by numerical simulations and offers a more flexible framework that can be applied to a broader range of situations, potentially leading to a more unified theoretical understanding of these materials.

Within the context of dense, isospin-saturated nuclear matter, consisting of neutrons, protons, and hyperons, we have determined the adiabatic index to be approximately 0.18 for neutron star densities. This value remains consistent across various models of strong interaction and strange stars. Moreover, we find that the speed of sound in dense matter is less than half the speed of light, meeting the basic requirements for dense matter stars as equations of state. Additionally, we establish relationships between the adiabatic index and other properties of compact stars. These findings hold significance for upcoming gravitational wave observations that will likely investigate the properties of dense matter stars in detail.

Researchers examine how to compare evolutionary trees based on the characteristics of the species they contain, specifically focusing on trees with the names of the species written on their branches. Existing methods of comparing trees rely on the ultrametric form, obtained by re-rooting and stretching them, and transform the comparison of trees into an isometry problem in metric spaces. This approach has limitations when dealing with large datasets, as it involves parameterizing the boundaries of the space of all possible trees. In contrast, a new method compares trees directly in their original form, using a novel metric that takes into account the names of the species and their evolutionary paths. This approach allows for the comparison of trees with non-biological characteristics, such as words or numbers, and demonstrates better performance in computational experiments.

We investigate a variety of discrete states within the Fock space using a simple, yet effective quadrature operator transformed through a displacement-squeezing transformation. To gain insight, we directly derive key properties, including the mean value of the number operator, its fluctuation, and the coherence. Notably, our analysis shows that squeezing contributes negatively to these quantities along the x-axis, whereas a positive impact is observed for the y-axis. Conversely, a displacement has the opposite effect, depending on the axis in question.

A phenomenon known as vertical shear instability (VSI) can occur in protoplanetary disk systems. It has the potential to impact the formation and development of planetesimals in the outer regions of these disks. In the presence of gas and dust particles, VSI's impact needs to be reassessed. This study aims to investigate how dust with varying properties affects VSI's growth rate and stability in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. The research indicates that VSI's growth rate is significantly reduced when considering dust particles, and this effect becomes more pronounced when dust concentrations increase. Additionally, VSI's impact on the disk can be minimized by accounting for the polymerization effects of sticking dust grains, which may also influence the vertical mixing of the disk.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and has constant scalar curvature. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold. Additionally, we have established a relevant theorem regarding the preservation of certain properties.

Sequential neural network models often employ dynamic mechanisms in their initial stages to adapt to input sequences of unequal length. We extend this concept to any layer within the network by proposing Dynamic Entrance Modules, a portable and flexible mechanism that allows multiple entry points within the sequence-based network. Additionally, we integrate Global Mean Pooling to combine local features and facilitate the dynamic learning of sequence representations. This approach is then applied to Bidirectional Recurrent Neural Networks through a Dynamic Entrance Bidirectional RNN framework, resulting in a model that adapts its input processing based on input sequence characteristics. Experimentally, our method achieves superior performance compared to static networks and alternative dynamic approaches on multiple dataset benchmarks, notably improving accuracy on various sequence classification tasks by an average of 6.5% on the SemEval 2017 Task 1 and 8.8% on the STreeC benchmark, with further potential applications and results available on request.

High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical deviations from general relativity's predictions, potentially significant in contexts like astrometry. The post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$ influences parallax measurements, especially when they are large, though typically it has minimal impact. Our research analyzes how uncertainties in $\gamma$ affect the Gaia satellite's parallax findings, focusing on areas of the sky where stars with known distances are located. We discovered that most of these stars fall within regions where $\gamma$'s effect on parallax is negligible, given Gaia's typical error margins. However, a smaller subset of these stars has parallax measurements that could be influenced by $\gamma$, and thus these stars may serve as useful test subjects for general relativity in the future.

We have developed a powerful new approach that uses high-fidelity simulations and observations from a system to create a highly simplified model, reducing dimensions and equations exponentially. This technique achieves remarkable speed and efficiency gains, overcoming significant challenges in applying dimensionality reduction methods to complex, rapidly evolving systems. By leveraging recent advances in machine learning that can work with equations rather than just numbers, our approach delivers a groundbreaking framework for applying techniques like principle component analysis to systems with multiple interacting components. By significantly reducing the number of variables needed to describe a system, we can make substantial improvements to how quickly and accurately we can predict a system's behavior, making our approach highly relevant to addressing some of the biggest challenges in science and engineering today.

In model systems featuring high-frequency modulations of potential, our analysis through both analytical and numerical methods reveals that initially localized waves in one-dimensional, multi-component Bose-Einstein condensates exhibit enhanced stability. This increased stability allows for the reduction of required initial conditions, enabling the creation of persistent, localized excitations even in the presence of group velocity mismatch between components. Our findings also indicate that this self-amplifying effect can lead to the formation of stable breathers through a weak modulation of the inter-atomic interaction, facilitating a transition from a soliton to a dimerized state.

This research proposes a breakthrough method to safeguard machine learning model confidentiality in scenarios where input data and model are shared with an untrusted entity. The proposed solution, SIMC 2.0, builds upon previous work by introducing an adaptable linear solver that addresses performance concerns and develops an efficient protocol for model updates in anticipation of future attacks. Key advancements include: optimizing computation for machine learning through floating point operations; designing a secure multi-party protocol for linear equations with dynamic participant roles; and a protocol for upsampling numerical data without compromising performance. Notably, our research reduces the average computational overhead associated with the secure training of machine learning models by nearly an order of magnitude.

Using the FAST radio telescope, we have significantly expanded our knowledge of the M101 galaxy group's HI structure. Our data shows that the system contains numerous HI clouds beyond its member galaxies, as well as a newly discovered HI tail extending over 110 kpc behind M101. This tail is likely a consequence of interaction between M101 and its nearby galaxy, NGC 5477. Additionally, we have found additional HI clouds at radii of approximately 150-300 kpc from M101's center, at velocities that align with the galaxy's HI envelope. These clouds may originate from a nearby galaxy group known as the M101 group's southern substructure, which was previously detected using the GBT.

To effectively handle questions that do not rely on factual knowledge but rather on general common sense, a category of questions that has not been fully addressed in Open-Domain Commonsense Question Answering platforms is the semantic-related question. Current approaches typically rely on retrieval-based strategies from a vast knowledge base, but this can lead to inaccurate answers due to the presence of noisy data. In contrast, our proposed framework called Coarse-to-Precise (C2P) takes a more targeted approach, beginning with a coarse classification of question types to guide a more focused search for answers from a semantically related commonsense knowledge graph. To enhance the accuracy of this approach, C2P incorporates two key components: a question-answer pairing classification model and a scoring model that assesses the semantic connection between questions and potential answers. In evaluating our method against existing approaches and a diverse set of question types, C2P demonstrates superior performance, achieving a notable increase in MRR score of 12% on the CommonsenseQA benchmark.

A crucial area in astrophysics, where knowledge is lacking, is the spectra of molecular cations containing oxygen in combination with other elements, specifically in regions of low temperature and density within comets and in the interstellar space. Although these species are expected to form rapidly after their parent molecule's formation in comets and in interstellar environments, and thus should be abundant, there is a lack of direct observations to verify this assumption. By calculating the equilibrium constants of oxygen-bearing molecular cations' formation in comets and in interstellar environments using astrophysical data, including temperatures, densities and the ages of these environments, researchers can determine if there are any necessary adjustments to the known energy levels of these cations. Additionally, a more accurate assessment can be made of the available theoretical and experimental data on the electronic spectra of these cations, with the goal of completing the existing knowledge in this field.

The totient sum of squares problem poses an interesting challenge, particularly evident when considering quadratic residues in global fields. This work explores an important aspect of that problem, focusing on the enumeration of elements with specific absolute values in number fields that are not rational. By establishing a one-to-one correspondence with elements in function fields, our approach allows us to leverage results on quadratic residues in function fields, ultimately yielding substantial insights when the field has a high degree of complexity. Our findings also reveal non-trivial connections between the totient sum of squares problem and the study of quadratic residues. Building upon this, we also address analogous problems related to norms of elements within number fields.

We're proposing a new method to tackle the anomaly detection problem, specifically in the field of astrophysics, using a unique combination of photonic neural networks and spectral matching techniques. Our approach builds upon existing methods by integrating a neural network that generates a set of template spectra from a limited number of reference star spectra. We utilize this neural network to compare the observed spectra of stars with their template spectra, leveraging spectral features to improve the accuracy of our predictions. The neural network's output is based on a combination of \chi^2 statistics and a metric that evaluates the similarity between observed and template spectra. We test our framework on real data, achieving a 24% reduction in loss and a 30% improvement in benchmark scores compared to state-of-the-art techniques, while also demonstrating a 50% increase in efficiency.

The precise monitoring of patients' medication intake is crucial for the effectiveness of pharmacotherapy, which can involve polypharmacy regimens consisting of multiple medications taken together. Due to the complexity of interacting medication interactions, adherence to individual medications can be impaired, which is a key reason for de-adherence in chronic diseases. To address this challenge, machine learning algorithms can be trained on vast amounts of literature and clinical trial data to predict the interactions between medications. Interaction prediction models are being explored in various studies, which often employ deep learning architectures to handle semantic representations of medications and their interactions. This study provides an in-depth analysis of these approaches, which are grounded in relational learning, which involves learning relationships between entities of different categories. We examine four primary architectures within this framework, which are then applied to a medication interaction prediction task. Our research involves designing and evaluating two novel models, a graph attention network and a mesh attention network, which are well-suited for medication interaction predictions. Our findings indicate that these models can achieve high accuracy in predicting interactions between medications that have been observed in clinical trials and literature. Moreover, they exhibit a robust performance in predicting interactions between medications that have not been observed before, which is critical for handling the complexity of medication interactions.

An Itô-Wentzell type equation is a second-order rough path controlled differential equation whose solutions rely on differentiating the raw signals, rather than lifting them to a higher dimension. We expand on previous work by establishing the existence and uniqueness of solutions to this type of equation when the signals have bounded variation. Additionally, we demonstrate that solutions can be represented through an explicit formula, analogous to a version for regular differential equations.

Federated learning enables multiple entities to collaborate on training a shared model. A significant challenge in FL is dealing with diverse data distributions across participating clients. We propose a novel random walk method to tackle this issue. In traditional machine learning, models are optimized to perform well on the training data. Conversely, our 'Stroll for Education' approach advocates for a more exploratory strategy, where the model's objective is to visit as many regions of the data space as possible. This is achieved by adapting the model to minimize a custom penalty function that assesses the frequency of visiting specific data points. Our experiments demonstrate that this approach yields compelling results for reducing the data distribution disparity and improving the model's performance on previously unseen data when compared to conventional federated learning methods.

New studies have confirmed the validity of a previously proven theoretical spectrum for rotating shear flows, specifically those with high levels of turbulence triggered by a periodically vibrating square located within an otherwise stationary viscous fluid.  The research involves analyzing and drawing conclusions from numerical experiments designed to examine inertial wave turbulence.  The schedule of the experiments, conducted on a cubic computer network, was structured to mimic the characteristics of turbulent wave behavior.  A duration of sixteen inertial periods was chosen for both short-scale (large amplitude) and long-scale (low amplitude) simulations, allowing researchers to obtain a direct spectrum by plotting the distribution of energy within the simulations against the corresponding angular frequency.  The schedule included the addition of small-scale simulations to study the natural dissipation of energy within the simulations, using a method that removes artificial effects of viscosity.  The schedule for the short-scale and long-scale simulations was compared to the known direct spectrum of an inertial wave turbulence spectrum, and the results showed a close match, thereby providing evidence for the applicability of this spectrum across a wide range of flows with moderate to high levels of turbulence.

Required mental health counseling for convicted offenders who have completed their sentences has been introduced in various forms in recent years in the United States. This research investigates the effectiveness of this approach by examining the positive impact of mandated therapy on this population's mental well-being. A randomized controlled trial was conducted, enrolling 500 participants who had undergone sentencing and were awaiting parole. Half were notified that mental health counseling would be a prerequisite for further consideration, with the other half serving as the control group. All participants underwent periodic mental health assessments throughout the trial duration. The findings indicate that convicted offenders who were informed that mental health counseling would be mandatory for their parole showed improved mental well-being compared to the control group. Additionally, those in the mandated therapy group exhibited lower rates of self-reported mental health issues and fewer incidents of violent behavior. These results provide insight into the benefits of mental health counseling for this specific demographic and the potential advantages of requiring mental health counseling as a condition of parole.

Medical image segmentation models are often developed with limited labeled data and must handle noise in both the training and inference phases.  To enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation, we suggest incorporating a regularization term that enforces consistency between the labels assigned to transformed versions of the images.  This technique requires neither the re-labeling of labeled data nor the generation of unlabelled data and is therefore effortless to implement.  Compared to alternative methods, our model yields higher quality segmentations as demonstrated on the MMWA dataset with a focus on cardiac muscle tissue segmentation, with a corresponding reduction in uncertainty and a more consistent distance between the predicted contours and ground truth.

To handle increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider in 2021, the ATLAS collaboration will undertake critical upgrades, including enhancing the Level 1 first trigger calculator. Specifically, the jet calorimeter trigger system demands significantly improved processing speed to effectively identify leading jets. To meet this need, we present a novel high-speed digital circuit built with use of an Ultrascale+ FPGA and capable of full-speed jet finding with an energy threshold, an approach that replicates the approach employed in the central electromagnetic trigger cluster processor. Building on previous work, our design has been optimized for larger FPGAs, incorporating lessons learned from the pilot phase, particularly in efficiently preventing overflow in the jet cell network by reordering the sequence of data processing. Furthermore, the design has been thoroughly tested for reliability and efficiency before being ready for mass production and integration into the final trigger system.

By combining neural networks with traditional graphics techniques, realistic virtual avatars can be created from sparse facial descriptions. Current approaches to generating highly detailed avatars from monocular input face images are limited in scope. Our novel Articulated Neural Visualization model addresses this constraint by creating a high-resolution, dynamic avatar representation from a single image in real-time. In contrast to rigid approaches, our model uses a mesh based on traditional morphable model technology to provide more realistic facial expressions and head rotations. It achieves this through a unique articulated mesh representation that is efficiently processed by a conventional ray marching method. When trained on a substantial dataset, our model exhibits exceptional performance in multiple evaluation metrics, surpassing state-of-the-art unified neural renderer models while offering more controllable and realistic avatars. Moreover, our model enables seamless integration with external articulations, such as voice-led facial animations.

Using our graph neural network model, which we've made transparent in methodology, we've analyzed and visualized data from experiments involving irradiated rubidium to demonstrate its computational capabilities. By applying this model, we've obtained a complex system's functional intermediate-layer representations, revealing how to effectively utilize neural network technology to interpret experimental observations from a quantum mechanics perspective. Additionally, we've derived a symbolic expression for a finite time's tomographic amplitudes using the NN's weights and demonstrated how to extract physical properties from the NN's multi-layered representations by analyzing an easy-to-grasp example. Furthermore, we've compared our approach to a general neural network framework, showing how our method's transparency provides a deeper understanding of the data processing involved.

Consider a statistical model with parameters that vary based on a unknown mixture component structure. When the number of observations is large, certain conditions apply, and the distribution of parameters follows a known form, typically an exponential family. Under these circumstances, an alternative, non-Bayesian approach can be used to estimate the population parameter by analyzing the maximum likelihood estimates from a large number of random samples. However, working with individual maximum likelihood estimates is often impractical due to the large sample size required. In this paper, we introduce an innovative method to assess the population parameter by combining information from a smaller number of larger samples. We derive conditions, discuss how to apply bootstrapping to assess precision, and provide theoretical guarantees for consistency and asymptotic normality. This method is particularly useful when working with large datasets, such as modern survey data, animal populations, or biological experiments with many treatments.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based approaches in the past few years. The success of these models has spurred interest in understanding their performance. To facilitate this comprehension, we introduce pyKT, a leading evaluation toolkit for deep learning-based knowledge tracing models. This framework provides essential tools to apply various rigorous evaluation methods, including synthetic control, causal effect estimation, and model-agnostic evaluation techniques. By leveraging pyKT, researchers can seamlessly assess the causal efficacy of their knowledge tracing models using a range of established techniques. Additionally, the framework supports custom-made protocol designs for both single and multiple model comparisons. pyKT is available on GitHub under the MIT License.

Let $\pi: X \to Y$ be a differentiable map between noncompact manifold $X$ and $Y$. Suppose that for every point $y \in Y$, the map $\pi$ induces a local diffeomorphism from a neighborhood of $y$ to a neighborhood of the corresponding point in $X$. Under this condition, we prove that forming the pullback map $X \to Y$ via $\pi$ results in a submersion, whose kernel has a finite dimension equal to the number of isolated points in $X$ where the map $\pi$ fails to be a local diffeomorphism.

We introduce Alethe, a proof assistant and SMT solver for first-order logic with tactics. Alethe's unique proof strategy combines recursive queries with a form of saturation, offering a versatile proof structure that accommodates both resolution-based and tableau-based provers. To manage proofs, Alethe uses a hybrid of its built-in solver and an external SMT library, thanks to the latest version of the SMT-LIB standard. Furthermore, Alethe's proofs can be easily exported to other SMT-LIB compliant provers.

As asynchronous FL becomes more practical for large-scale and diverse distributed datasets, it's essential to address synchronization issues and optimize performance. Thestandard approach, synchronizing gradients across devices, can lead to slow convergence and limited training freedom. To overcome these challenges, this research proposes a new method called Buffered Asynchronous Accumulation (BAA) for unconstrained gradient updating in FL. In traditional FL frameworks, gradients are clipped to prevent overfitting when data is not synchronized, but this restriction hinders convergence in asynchronous training. The BAA method stores accumulated gradients from each device over time and uses these buffered results for optimization, eliminating the need for synchronous clipping. Theoretical and practical benefits of BAA were tested and the approach showed improved performance, faster convergence, and greater flexibility in model parameter updates. Comparison with alternative methods confirmed BAA's superiority in asynchronous FL applications.

Lately, single-model automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, largely due to the large amounts of training data available. Nonetheless, when faced with unfamiliar speakers or new languages, speech recognition relies on transferring knowledge from trained models. In this regard, we explore transferring knowledge across different languages and speaker categories by leveraging trained models, with an emphasis on a particular scenario involving a German speaker transcribing French text. Our primary findings show that using pre-trained multilingual models leads to superior performance compared to models specifically designed for low-resource languages. Furthermore, we discovered that training a model on a diverse set of languages does not necessarily enable it to handle unfamiliar languages in speech recognition tasks. In addition, incorporating unlabelled data improves performance in speech recognition tasks, including those involving unseen speakers. Our best approach involved training a model on a diverse range of languages and utilizing unlabelled data to adapt it to new speaker categories.

Graph neural network (GNN) node representations can be created using two methods: Proximity Preserving Graph Neural Networks (PP-GNNs) and Structural Role-based Graph Neural Networks (SR-GNNs). Despite the lack of suitable evaluation benchmarks, our proposed dataset, Twitch Players, addresses this limitation. It comprises 18 features and a binary classification target, where entities are accurately represented through their structural roles. Twitch Players data cannot be effectively modeled with traditional GNNs, requiring the use of sophisticated techniques such as multi-layer perceptrons and graph attention networks. Our findings indicate that SR-GNNs outperform PP-GNNs in this context.

Our study seeks to resolve the nature of the $f_X(1500)$ resonance observed in hadronic decays of B mesons. By utilizing a series of perturbative QCD diagrams with effective field theory for the $B\to \pi(K)KK$ process, we derive a specific, understandable form for the amplitude and find a clear, explicit expression for the resonance $f_X(1500)$. We find that if $f_X(1500)$ is a resonance of this process, it is very likely a continuation of the $\rho^0(1450)$ found in hadronic decays of $\tau$ mesons, specifically in the $h^0\pi^0$ and $\eta\eta$ decay modes, which is also observable in $B\to \pi(K)KK$ decays. This conclusion is reached by considering various initial and final state interactions in the $B\to \pi(K)KK$ process, which allows us to connect the results to those for the $\tau$ decay, leading to a more comprehensive understanding of the resonance's properties.

Researchers propose that a theory of gravity with higher dimensions exists, specifically proposing that one of those dimensions must be compactified in a way that results in a length smaller than the Planck length, essentially a "shadow dimension." They suggest that dark matter could be explained by the presence of primordial black holes formed right after the Big Bang, and that their gravitational effect is influenced by the existence of this higher dimension. Further, they contend that if this theory of gravity with extra dimensions applies to our universe, it would have far-reaching implications, requiring a significant portion of dark energy to be composed of objects more massive than the Sun, and that we should be able to observe a specific range of X-rays that would provide evidence for this theory.

A novel algorithm for precise force control in series elastic actuators is introduced in this paper, centered on a novel force observer technique. Traditionally, force control in SEAs relies on the elastic modulus of the material used in its elastic component for gain calculation, but this method is often impractical due to the many variables affecting SEA behavior, including stiffening effects, actuator saturation, and time-domain characteristics. An alternative approach presented in this work utilizes a transmission force observer, leveraging the SEA's forward dynamics to estimate its behavior, and has been successfully tested on an experimental setup using an elastic joint and a high-gain position controller. The results show that this algorithm can accurately minimize and reject disturbances in response to changing loads and frequencies.

A raft made of a brittle material that's subjected to tension will inevitably crack, and this damage propagates in various possible ways. This research aims to examine how a raft's fracture pattern is influenced by the location and size of inclusions within it. It's known that inclusions can significantly impact the stress distribution within the raft, creating areas of high tension that could potentially dictate the path of crack development. By running numerous simulations with varying inclusion positions and sizes, this study creates a comprehensive map of possible fracture patterns that result from different stress distributions. This map of fractures provides valuable insights that could also be applied to other types of structures that feature inclusions, such as pavement systems.

We studied a range of SU(Nc) gauge theories in three dimensions, incorporating a variety of multicomponent scalar fields with different symmetries, situated within a discrete lattice framework. Through thermal tuning, we investigated the phase transitions from the symmetric phase to symmetry-breaking phases characterized by Higgs states. Our analysis revealed distinct symmetry-breaking patterns corresponding to different equilibrium Higgs states. Furthermore, our findings indicated that specific thermal phase transitions could lead to the formation of multiple Higgs states, thereby demonstrating the complexity of thermal phase transitions in these gauge theories.

To enhance marine robot navigation using sensory data, our novel approach introduces a new method for extracting relevant time-based pattern information from sensor signals. By combining Gaussian Process regression with a sparsity-promoting prior, our algorithm efficiently discovers and models significant changes in signal variations over time. The proposed method is easy to implement, computationally straightforward, and effectively captures important temporal variation features in comparison to more complex methods. Our results demonstrate that incorporating the algorithm into marine robot navigation using sensory data leads to superior performance.

This paper introduces a novel neural network design called Arrangement Networks (ANets) to perform outstandingly on both linear and nonlinear classification tasks. ANets leverage attention mechanisms to weigh input features and compute decision boundaries through linear functions, including those of higher degrees. Notably, ANets achieve state-of-the-art performance on the binary and multi-class versions of the Permutation Invariant Classification (PIC) benchmark.

We're investigating a novel class of relativistic, anisotropic stars that maintain their structure in an environment filled with a surrounding fluid of greater energy density. Our research focuses on the relationship between the pressure of the star and its internal energy, constrained by the condition that the star's surface must remain stable. Building upon an earlier proposal, we're exploring specific arrangements where the pressure and energy relationship takes the form of a linear function, as well as a new scenario where this relationship is defined by a quadratic equation. Our primary goal is to identify the specific configurations that satisfy the stability condition at the star's surface.

Using semi-analytical models and computer simulations, a study has examined how a galaxy similar to the Milky Way, with multiple spiral arms, forms and evolves. A computer simulation was used to model a large section of the galaxy's central region, focusing on how spiral arms are created and the patterns of star formation within them. Researchers discovered that a region within the galaxy's central area, where gas and star density is highest, develops an irregular spiral arm structure due to the gravitational pull of an outer bar. This finding provides insight into the development of the Milky Way's spiral arms. Additionally, a section of the galaxy was modeled after looking down its central plane, revealing a spiral arm pattern that resembles the Sagittarius A* region of the Milky Way. Further research is being done to study how a galaxy's central region changes over time.

This research explores the impact of massive magnetic fields on galaxy mergers in an expanding universe. We developed a new set of simulations, adapting the methods used in the RAMSES code to incorporate the influence of magnetic fields on gas and star movements. We applied these simulations to examine how magnetic fields shape galaxy interactions and mergers. In our simulations, we found that massive magnetic fields restrict the formation of supermassive halos and impede the flow of gas during galaxy interactions. As a result, we observed that galaxy mergers in our simulations lacked the massive, ring-like structures typically created when galaxy interactions are unaffected by magnetic fields. Instead, we found that magnetic fields in galaxy mergers lead to increased star creation in the central galaxy region and more substantial, disk-like structure formation. We also discovered that the strength of magnetic fields has a comparable effect to that of weakly ionized gas in galaxy mergers, although it has a greater impact when galaxy interactions are more vigorous. We anticipate that our findings will be confirmed by more complex simulations and that our research will contribute to a better understanding of magnetic field influence in galaxy evolution.

Our solution to the 2nd COVID-19 Severity Detection Competition has been successfully presented, where our goal was to classify chest CT scans as Mild, Moderate, Severe, or Critical COVID-19 cases.  Our approach, called Infection-aware Contrastive Mixup Classification (ICMC), achieved top rankings in both task 1 (Moderate-Severe classification) and task 2 (Mild-Critical classification), outperforming baseline models and top-entry submissions on severity-specific evaluation metrics.  For example, in task 1, our method ranked 1st with a DICE coefficient of 0.8143, while in task 2, ICMC secured 1st place with a DICE coefficient of 0.8135.  We further validated CT scan and MRI scan data, demonstrating competitive performance against leading competition submissions with mean dice coefficients of 0.7926 and 0.7851 respectively.  A key innovation of our approach involves the introduction of mixup-based classification methods, particularly cross-patient mixup and infection-aware contrastive learning, both of which have not been applied to medical image classification in previous research.

Most current research focusing on grammatical error rectification has concentrated on standard supervised learning models, utilizing vast amounts of labeled data to train them. Nonetheless, labeling datasets for grammatical errors is extremely time-consuming, especially in new domains, where resources might be ample but labeled data is scarce. Consequently, developing methods that can quickly adapt to new domains without needing extensive labeling becomes essential. In this paper, we propose leveraging meta-learning to achieve such domain adaptation. We introduce a meta-facilitated agent that learns from experience in multiple practice domains and subsequently transfers that knowledge to new target domains with limited labeling. Results indicate that this approach yields highly competitive performance on previously unseen domains, notably outperforming the baseline model trained on a single target domain by a margin of 10.14% in F1 score. Furthermore, our model's ability to adapt across domains with substantially reduced labeling requirements is critically examined, revealing a notable reduction of 24.53% in needed labels.

Rounding on surveys can lead to uncertainty when respondents answer questions that aren't straightforward, as the true value may fall anywhere between two integers. Typically, researchers treat rounded answers as accurate to a range of one unit, but often fail to consider this ambiguity when calculating totals from rounded averages. In many cases, the standard error formula overlooks this ambiguity, which can significantly impact estimates, especially when rounded averages are used to calculate totals through counts of individual items. Our analysis assesses the impact of this ambiguity using different standard error formulas and finds that it can substantially increase the margin of error, sometimes by as much as five times the usual amount. This concept is illustrated using data from student mathematics competency surveys in Oregon's schools. Our study also explores the effect of different rounding schemes on estimates of totals and finds that the choice of standard error formula has implications for statistical significance, with some formulas producing findings that align with those from an unrounded version of the data. Our research ultimately suggests that when rounding schemes allow for ambiguity, a more accurate standard error formula should be used to account for this effect on estimates of totals.

Researchers investigated the crystal and magnetic characteristics of GdInO3, a material that only exists in a highly oxygen-deficient state. They studied its structure, found to be centered on a honeycomb lattice, and found a very low value for the magnetic exchange interaction constant in this direction. Using various techniques, they found that magnetic ordering occurs at a very low temperature and characterized its structure. Additionally, they observed a unique shift in some peaks in the infrared spectrum. Furthermore, we found that magnetic ordering can be explained by a mean-field approach, and calculated the strength of the magnetic exchange interaction in the honeycomb lattice.

The problem of trading indivisible items for self-interested, rational agents with complete information has a well-known formulation as combinatorial auctions. Our study offers an original contribution to this area by exploring new concepts. We introduce a new combinatorial auction model, referred to as Equity-Dominated Combinatorial Auctions, which ensures that any equilibrium outcome where all agents are satisfied must adhere to the rule that the distribution of items remains equitable compared to the initial state. In our investigation, we focus on identifying and characterizing pure Nash equilibria within this new framework, using a specific instance of Equity-Dominated Combinatorial Auctions. Specifically, we examined Equity-Dominated Single-Item Auctions, a simplified version where each agent has an individual item they wishes to acquire, and demonstrated that it is possible to determine the set of pure Nash equilibria by employing Graph Matching. Furthermore, we conducted an in-depth analysis to determine whether our approach can be applied to more complex scenarios, and discussed both the challenges and opportunities arising from our results. Our work on Equity-Dominated Combinatorial Auctions has the advantage of linking pure Nash equilibria with the concept of item equity, a feature that can be applied to various other Equity-Dominated Combinatorial Auctions scenarios.

When adapting to a new domain in an unsupervised setting for transfer learning, most current methods overlook the possibility of having multiple possible scenarios. Unlike these approaches, our proposed framework is more adaptable as it can handle various situations that may arise when adjusting to a new domain. Instead of focusing solely on ideal cases, our model is designed to recognize both domain-specific patterns and the differences between them. When applying this to image classification using the Domain Adaptation Protocol, our results show that our proposed model outperforms the current state-of-the-art by a significant margin. Moreover, our model's code and model are publicly available for download.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation and meager molecular gas content. A comprehensive study of this galaxy involves a hitherto unexplored one-kpc radio continuum project, aided by high-resolution radio observations using the VLA. The research reveals a vast, highly stable radio disk in UGC 8839, extending far beyond its optical boundary. The large disk exhibits little to no signs of interaction with the galaxy's central region, an anomaly given typical local alignments in spiral galaxies. Furthermore, observations of extremely low star formation rates across 24 $\mu$m infrared dark features in the disk of UGC 8839 suggest a lack of gas dynamics that could contribute to its unusual stability.

Researchers propose using paleo-detectors, ancient geological formations with high sensitivity to ionizing radiation, to investigate dark matter interactions with nucleons and other particles. If low-energy dark matter interactions are significant, they may result in the radiative excitation of electrons within these formations, potentially producing characteristic signals such as increased radiation in certain energy ranges. Furthermore, this approach can distinguish between different types of dark matter based on their masses, densities, and speeds. Additionally, paleo-detectors can provide more stringent constraints on the parameters of certain models, such as RGE extended standard model, and offer complementary insights to other dark matter detection methods.

Research into modern database encryption techniques focuses on addressing update pattern attacks representing a significant risk in cloud-based storage. Update pattern analysis enables an attacker to deduce sensitive information despite encryption, potentially compromising confidentiality when using frequency-based schemes. Our proposed DP-Sync method incorporates differential privacy to prevent such attacks, ensuring the protection of frequency lists against skilled adversaries. By integrating the private synthetic frequency learning algorithm, DP-Sync conceals update patterns, making it possible to safely lease database storage to trusted and untrusted users. Our experimental results demonstrate DP-Sync's effectiveness in preventing frequency learning attacks in real-world scenarios.

Features used in machine learning that are not relevant can negatively impact model performance and stability.
